Title candidates ([PENDING], pick one or none): 1. We wanted 1000 players on one server. The first build broke near 190. Here's why everyone stops near 64. 2. Why realtime games cap at ~64–150 players, measured on a $7.59 server 3. The N² wall: load-testing a bit-packed Rust game server

0. Cold open: five ramps, one wall

We asked a small ARM server for 200 players. It reached 191 before new players started timing out. We asked for 250 and it reached 185. Then 500 gave 176, 750 gave 180, and 999 gave 190.

Five join ramps, five requested sizes spread over a factor of five, and every one of them stopped in the same 15-player band. The server was a Hetzner CAX11: two shared Arm vCPUs, 4 GB of RAM, in Falkenstein, quoted at the time at $6.99 a month plus $0.60 for an IPv4 address, $7.59 a month. A second CAX11 in the same zone ran the bots. (Original checkpoint.)

[AUTHOR] The $7.59 is the historical conditional quote retained by the campaign, not a verified current price. Keep it as "quoted at the time".

The failure had the same shape every time. First the game host's kernel started dropping UDP datagrams because the socket's receive buffer was full. That happened at 131–164 players, while the game process was using only 57–76% of one core. Later the process CPU climbed to about one full core, players dropped, new joins timed out, and the controller aborted.

That band sits right next to the numbers the industry ships. Warzone launched at 150 players. PlanetSide 2 caps a continent at 250 per faction. Star Citizen ran about 100 per server before server meshing. Battlefield, after trying 128, went back to 64. Is that a coincidence?

This article argues it isn't. The cap falls out of arithmetic, and you can watch the arithmetic happen in our own bytes.

One warning before we start: 191, 185, 176, 180 and 190 are the peak connected-player counts from those five attempts, not sustainable player capacities. Each test gradually added bots—a "join ramp"—toward its requested population. All five failed before reaching the five-minute measurement window. The data supports "our first build's attempts to fill the server broke around 180–190 authenticated players." It doesn't establish that a $7.59 server can reliably sustain 190 players.

Eight days later, after a round of correctness fixes to the server, the client and our own measurement code, a fixed build held 150 players for five clean minutes. Its 200-player attempt failed in a way we couldn't measure, because the bot host was dropping packets too. So the fixed build's ceiling is unknown, and saying so is part of the story.

1. What Omega is, and what we set out to prove

Omega Realm is a top-down 2D bullet-hell shooter. Its gameplay is minimal on purpose: three Classes, a shooting attack and one ability each, HP and nothing else, and one monster type. The game exists to stress-test netcode. The question behind it is whether one server Instance (one running copy of a map) can hold 500–1000 concurrent realtime players.

The architecture, in one paragraph:

  • omega-server is a Rust binary with a single-threaded, fixed 30 Hz Tick. One thread runs the simulation, services the network, encodes Snapshots and flushes them.
  • Transport is ENet over UDP, through the rusty_enet crate pinned at 0.4.0 (a Rust transpile of ENet 1.3.18). There are three channels: ch0 unreliable sequenced (Snapshots, input confirms), ch1 reliable ordered (Baselines, Game events, auth), ch2 unreliable sequenced (client input).
  • A Rust crate, sim_core, holds movement, collision and hit logic. The server runs it, and the Godot client runs the same compiled code for prediction through a GDExtension, so the two can't diverge.
  • The governing rule: the client requests, the server decides.

The rest of the article uses a few terms exactly:

Term Meaning here
Tick One step of the server's authoritative simulation. Ours is 30 Hz, so 33.3 ms.
Frame One client render. Not a Tick.
Snapshot One replicated world-state message from the server to one client. Ours go out once per Tick.
Baseline A full-state Snapshot that later delta Snapshots are encoded against.
AoI Area of Interest: the region around a player whose entities that player is sent.
Game event A one-shot authoritative occurrence (shot fired, damage, kill), separate from Snapshots.
Instance One running copy of a map. The load tests use one Arena Instance, 2000 × 2000 units.

This article doesn't cover how the game feels: prediction, interpolation and render smoothness are separate work. It is about how many players one Instance can carry, and why.

2. The ceiling everyone hits

Look at enough realtime games and the same picture comes up. Player caps aren't usually set by one hard limit. They come from a fixed CPU budget per Tick (1/tick-rate seconds, shared by however many matches you pack onto a core) set against per-Tick work that grows faster than N. Studios trade tick rate against player count against matches per core, then pick a design number somewhere below the technical ceiling.

Game Players Tick / update rate What the studio said Tag
Quake III Arena (1999) MAX_CLIENTS 64 // absolute limit sv_fps 20 Hard-coded in q_shared.h [P]
Source engine (2004–) 32 by design, 255 absolute 66.67 "really designed for 32 or less players" (SDK shareddefs.h) [P]
Apex Legends (2019) 60 20 Hz ~60 kB/s per client; 60 Hz "would consume 180kB/s" (Respawn) [P]
Valorant (2020) 10 128 ≥3 games per core, 2.34 ms per frame (Riot) [P]
Fortnite (2017) 100 20 → 30 Hz Per-actor-per-client relevancy "will bottleneck the server's CPU" (Epic) [P]
Warzone (2020) 150 → 100 → 120 ~20 Hz (community) 150 "works best for the mode" (Charlie INTEL) [S]
Battlefield 4 (2013) 64 30 default, ≤60 at 64 players 64 players: one Instance per box, 60 Hz max (DICE PDF) [P]
Battlefield 6 REDSEC (2025) 100+ 30 Hz, "60hz for the final fight" "They were not running 100 players" (Insider Gaming) [S]
Star Citizen 4.0 (2024) ~100 per server, 500 per shard n/p Server meshing splits authority across processes (RSI) [S]

Tags: [P] primary source read directly, [S] first-party statement read through the press, [D] our arithmetic. The full 20-row table, with every source, is in realtime-player-caps.md.

The cleanest number in the set: Valorant

Riot published the arithmetic. At 128 Hz a Tick lasts 7.8125 ms. Riot needed better than three games per core to make hosting affordable ("a single game per core would be prohibitively expensive"), and reserved 10% for the OS, which left 2.34 ms per game per Tick for 10 players. A 36-core host runs 108 games, or 1,080 players. (Riot, 128-tick servers.)

D1, the yardstick [D]. 1,080 players ÷ 36 cores = 30 players per core at 128 Hz, or 30 × 128 = 3,840 player-Ticks per core-second. Rescaled naively to 30 Hz, that is 3,840 / 30 = 128 players per core. We'll hold our own numbers up against this in §7. The rescale is naive on purpose: it assumes per-player cost is constant in N, and the rest of this article is about why it isn't.

Why the work grows faster than N

The recurring reasons, in rough order of how often studios name them:

  1. Relevance fan-out is O(N²) per Tick. Every player is both an observer and something observed. If everyone is relevant to everyone, the server must decide, serialise and send about N × (N − 1) entity records per Tick. Epic's Replication Graph exists because stock Unreal replication checks every actor against every connection, which at Fortnite's 100 players and ~50,000 actors "will bottleneck the server's CPU" (Epic).
  2. The CPU budget per Tick is fixed. Overrun it and the tick rate drops, or the clock dilates.
  3. Lag-compensated hits multiply with N. Source keeps "a history of all recent player positions for one second" and rewinds "all other players" for every shot (Valve wiki). The work per shot grows with N, and so does the number of shots.
  4. Downstream bandwidth per client grows with visible entities × rate. Apex measured about 60 kB/s per client at 20 Hz and said 60 Hz would mean 180 kB/s: "for triple the bandwidth and CPU costs, you can save two frames worth of latency" (Respawn).
  5. A Snapshot wants to fit in one datagram. Lose one fragment of an unreliable Snapshot and the whole Snapshot is gone. Quake III caps packets at 1,400 B; Valve's GameNetworkingSockets at 1,300 B.

Two pressures sit on top. Players now expect 60–128 Hz, and every doubling of tick rate halves the per-Tick budget. And the weakest client still has to render, animate and simulate every visible character: EA kept last-gen consoles at 64 players in Battlefield 2042 to keep "performance stable for older systems" (EA FAQ).

Battlefield: 64 as a design choice, paid for in tick rate

Battlefield is the useful counterexample, because DICE has said in public that the engine could go higher.

  • 2011, DICE CEO Patrick Söderlund: "Technically, we can go to 256, we've tried it. We play tested with 128." And: "tested 128 and that it's not fun… there's no point in going higher than 64." (GameRevolution, [S])
  • Battlefield 2042 shipped 128-player modes, then removed 128-player Breakthrough in Update 4.1 because "the value and impact of an individual player, and squad is reduced due to the increased intensity and chaos of the combat" (EA patch notes, [P]). Battlefield 6 went back to 64 because 128 "didn't catch on" (PC Gamer via inkl, [S]).

No first-party DICE or EA source gives CPU or bandwidth as the reason for 64. But the tax is visible in the tick rate. DICE's 2015 guidance for Battlefield 4 high-tickrate servers, verbatim (EA-hosted PDF, [P]):

  • "For 64 player servers we recommend a single instance per hardware, limiting max tickrate to 60hz"
  • "For 48/32 player slots we recommend half the number of instances running per hardware (normally translates to 2 instances instead of 4 per server)"; "limiting the max tickrate to 120hz"
  • "Normally, servers in Battlefield 4 run at 30hz"

[D] The "normally 4" is the density at the 30 Hz default. So per box, 4 × 64 × 30 = 7,680 player-Ticks per second at 30 Hz, against 1 × 64 × 60 = 3,840 at 60 Hz. Doubling the tick rate of a 64-player server costs four times the hardware per match, not two. That is what you expect when each player's Snapshot covers every other player: cost goes as N · k · f, and k ≈ N − 1.

Why is k ≈ N − 1 in Battlefield? Because the game is built that way. Open combined-arms maps, jets, artillery and long sightlines mean a player can see, spot, shell or be shot by most of the server. The only first-party relevance mechanism we found is Battlefield 4's 2014 "High Frequency Bubble", which sends more often to players inside a radius (Battlelog, [P]). It changes the rate. It isn't a cull. Nothing first-party says Battlefield ever stops sending distant players.

So DICE's levers are N (picked on design grounds) and f (picked on cost grounds). REDSEC, the Battlefield 6 battle royale, shows both at once: 100+ players at 30 Hz, stepping up to 60 Hz "for the final fight" once most players are dead (Sirland).

[AUTHOR] The reading "DICE picks N on design and f on cost" is our inference from the sources, not a DICE statement. Say so in the rewrite. Details: Battlefield/Rust research note.

The tech sets the ceiling, design picks the point

The public reason for a cap is very often design, even where the tech could go higher. MAG picked 256 "for game design reasons" and said its architecture "could increase the number players well beyond" (PlayStation Blog). Raven moved Warzone to 100 for "time-to-action, the map size… circle timings… total match time" (TechRadar, [S]). The networking ceiling decides whether a number is possible. Design decides where under it to land.

The few games that get well past ~150 do it by changing the rules. Star Citizen splits a world across server processes (500 players across 8–10 servers is about 50–60 per process [D]). EVE slows its game clock to 10% speed. Tab-target MMOs change what combat needs from the network. §4 takes those apart. First, the arithmetic.

3. The math of sending a world to N players

This section derives the formulas. The point it builds to: bit-packing and delta compression are constant factors. Only AoI changes the exponent. The full derivations, with every RFC and source-file reference, are in replication-math.md; the formula sheet is Appendix A.

Symbol Meaning
N connected players on one Instance
k entities in one client's Snapshot (its visible set)
b_e bits per entity record
H_s Snapshot header bytes (per datagram)
H_d per-datagram overhead below the game (IP + UDP + ENet)
f Snapshot rate, Hz
L max game payload per datagram
d datagrams per Snapshot

D2: what each datagram costs before your first byte

An unreliable ENet message alone in an IPv4 datagram carries:

H_d = IPv4 20 + UDP 8 + ENet header 2 + SEND_UNRELIABLE command 8 = 38 B

The 20 and 8 come from RFC 791 and RFC 768. The ENet sizes come from the #[repr(C, packed)] structs in rusty_enet 0.4.0, which match upstream protocol.h. ENet's header grows to 4 B when the datagram carries a reliable command, so the worst case on IPv6 (40 B header, RFC 8200) is 40 + 8 + 4 + 8 = 60 B.

That overhead is fixed per send, so it dominates small packets. Our 22-byte input packet is 38 / (22 + 38) = 63% header on IPv4. A 1,200-byte Snapshot is 3.1% header.

D3: where "1200 bytes" comes from

IPv6 requires every link to carry at least 1,280 octets (RFC 8200 §5). Subtract the worst-case headers:

L_max = 1280 − 40 (IPv6) − 8 (UDP) − 4 (ENet header) − 8 (SEND_UNRELIABLE) = 1220 B

So L = 1200 B leaves 20 B spare on the strictest legal path. QUIC derives the same rule from the same numbers (RFC 9000 §14), and Glenn Fiedler gives the same game-side advice: 1,000–1,200 bytes of payload (Gaffer On Games). ENet's own fragmentation threshold is higher, at 1392 − 4 − 24 = 1,364 B, and an unreliable packet above it becomes reliable fragments by default. That's the head-of-line-blocking trap a 1,200-byte cap protects against.

D4: bits per number

A value in a range of width range, sent with step q, needs

bits(range, q) = ceil( log2( range / q + 1 ) )

Our Arena is 2,000 units wide, quantized to 0.1 u: ceil(log2(20,001)) = 15 bits. We send 16 (an i16), one bit over the minimum. Each 10× gain in precision costs about log2(10) ≈ 3.3 bits per component.

D5: downstream per client, and egress for the server

records per datagram   r = floor( (L − H_s) · 8 / b_e )
datagrams per Snapshot d = ceil( k / r )
down per client        D = f · ( ceil(k · b_e / 8) + d · (H_s + H_d) )
server egress          E = N · D

Drop the per-datagram terms and the headline is bytes/s ≈ k × bytes per entity × f, per client. Then:

  • Naive broadcast, everyone sees everyone: k = N − 1, so E = Θ(N²). Going from 64 to 1000 players multiplies N(N − 1) by 999,000 / 4,032 = 248×.
  • AoI, each client only gets entities within radius R. With uniform density ρ = N / A, k ≈ min(N − 1, ρπR², k_max), and E = Θ(N · k). Once k saturates, egress is linear in N.

One case, step by step [D]. N = 1000 at 30 Hz, naive broadcast, our full 63-bit player record, IPv4, H_s = 12 B:

k = 999
r = floor((1200 − 12) × 8 / 63)      = 150 records per datagram
d = ceil(999 / 150)                   = 7 datagrams per Snapshot
payload P = 6 × (12 + 1182) + (12 + 780) = 7,956 B
wire W = P + 7 × 38                    = 8,222 B per Snapshot
D = 30 × 8,222                         = 246.7 kB/s ≈ 1.97 Mbit/s per client
E = 1000 × D                           ≈ 1,973 Mbit/s ≈ 2.0 Gbit/s
datagrams/s = 1000 × 7 × 30            = 210,000

With AoI capped at 64 entities, the same Instance needs d = 1, W = 554 B, D = 16.6 kB/s, and E ≈ 133 Mbit/s: 14.8× less, close to the asymptotic 999 / 64 = 15.6×.

F2 data: server egress vs N, our 63-bit records [D]. Players only; projectiles and monsters add on top with the same formula.

N 30 Hz naive 30 Hz AoI-64 60 Hz naive 60 Hz AoI-64 Datagrams/s, 30 Hz naive
16 0.6 Mbit/s 0.6 1.3 1.3 480
32 2.3 2.3 4.5 4.5 960
64 8.4 8.4 16.8 16.8 1,920
100 19.9 13.3 39.8 26.6 3,000
150 44.1 19.9 88.1 39.9 4,500
200 80.1 26.6 160.1 53.2 12,000
500 495.8 66.5 991.7 133.0 60,000
1000 1,973.3 133.0 3,946.6 265.9 210,000
F2 · original figure brief

[FIGURE F2 — new] Plot the four egress columns against N on log–log axes. The naive lines have slope 2, the AoI-64 lines bend to slope 1 at N = 65. Mark 1 Gbit/s as a horizontal line.

How to read it:

  • Tick rate is linear. 30 → 60 Hz doubles everything.
  • Bit-packing is a constant factor. Going from a naive 16-byte record (u16 id, three f32, u16 state) to our 63 bits saves about 2×. Delta compression adds about 1.25× more when everything moves (§5).
  • AoI is the only lever that changes the exponent. At 1000 players, naive broadcast needs 2–4 Gbit/s of egress at 30–60 Hz, more than one 1 Gbit/s port. AoI-64 needs 0.13–0.27 Gbit/s.
  • Packets per second matter too. ENet sends at least one datagram per peer per flush, so the floor is N × f datagrams per second, and every one is a syscall and kernel work. Naive 1000 at 60 Hz is 420,000 datagrams per second.

D6: the transfer bill

1 Gbit/s sustained is 125 MB/s × 2,592,000 s ≈ 324 TB per 30-day month. So even the AoI-64 case at 133 Mbit/s is about 43 TB a month. Many VPS plans meter transfer in single-digit TB, so the egress bill can bind before the link speed does.

The CPU side of the same formula

Bandwidth is only half of it. The work per Tick is roughly

C_tick ≈ C_sim(N, projectiles)       movement, collision, hit checks
       + N · C_aoi                   each client's visible-set query
       + Σ_i k_i · c_rec              serialise k records per recipient   → O(N · k)
       + N · d · c_send               ENet framing and one sendto() per datagram

against a budget of 1000 / f_tick ms: 33.3 ms at 30 Hz. Record writes per Tick are N · k: 999,000 for naive 1000 players, 64,000 with AoI-64. The per-record cost c_rec isn't a citable constant (it depends on your encoder), but as an illustration only, at 50 ns per record naive 1000 players costs about 50 ms per Tick in serialisation alone. That blows the 30 Hz budget on one thread before the simulation has run. AoI-64 costs about 3.2 ms.

Two caveats

Delta compression buys less than you'd hope in a shooter. Delta encoding sends only what changed since a Baseline. In a bullet hell almost everything moves every Tick, so you still send almost every position. Our position-only delta record is 49 bits against a 63-bit full record: a 22% saving when everyone moves. It pays off on slow fields (flags, animation, HP) and idle entities, not on positions.

AoI isn't magic. If everyone crowds into one radius (a boss fight, a town square), ρπR² → N and you're back at Θ(N²). Only a hard cap on k (a byte budget plus priorities) bounds that case. Plan capacity for the crowd, not the average.

The real-world AoI example: Rust's 1000-player servers

Rust (Facepunch) is the game people point to when they say a realtime game can hold 1000 on one server. It does, and the math says why. The details are in the Battlefield/Rust research note.

  • The relevance model is a hard spatial cull. Facepunch, 2014: "the world is divided into a grid for network reasons. A player is only sent the objects in adjacent cells" (Devblog 16, [P]). Cells are 32 m and the default far radius is 8 cells, so the subscribed area is a 544 m square whose corners reach about 360 m. Facepunch calls about 350 m "the size of a default network grid" (Maintenance, [P]). Terrain occlusion culls further.
  • Facepunch keeps R small on purpose. On extending the network range at sea: "We can't afford to do that on the mainland because of player and entity density" (Shipshape, [P]).

[D] k for players. A 4,500 m map is 20.25 km² (including ocean). At N = 1000, ρ ≈ 49 players per km². With R = 256–350 m, k = ρπR² ≈ 10–19 players. Assume only half the map is land and it doubles to 20–38. Against N − 1 = 999, that is a 26–98× cut. Even a 100-player crowd at one monument only raises k for those 100 clients; total replication work stays about 40× below naive broadcast.

Three qualifications keep this honest:

  1. Rust's "1000" is a wipe-day peak. Facepunch's own servers cap at 250–400. Community servers that touch 1,000–1,600 on wipe day average 150–340 over the week ([O], Rustalyzer, 2026-10-15).
  2. Rust's k is dominated by entities, not players. Servers hold 150,000–362,299 entities (bases, deployables, drops) ([P]). The 2026 per-entity network ranges exist to shrink entity k.
  3. The limit Facepunch reports is server CPU per frame, not bandwidth. "We spend about 19ms to process all 200 connected players in a server tick" (Crafting Update, [P]). And bandwidth is small: one commit saved ~105 KB/s, described as 6%, on a 122-player server, which implies about 14.3 kB/s per player [D]. At 1000 players that is roughly 115 Mbit/s, far inside one port.

So AoI is what moves Rust from Θ(N²) to Θ(N · k). It gets 1000 players past the bandwidth wall. It doesn't get them past the CPU wall, which in Facepunch's own numbers sits at a few hundred. Rust also escapes the fixed-Tick budget: there is no global Tick, and server FPS is allowed to sag (25–98 observed). Battlefield, at the other end, sets k = N − 1 by design and pays in f.

4. How tab-target MMOs put hundreds on screen

If the math is that harsh, how does World of Warcraft put 1,500 players in one zone? The short answer: it doesn't beat N². It pays it less often, per entity, and it designs combat that tolerates the server being late. Full sources: mmo-scaling-tab-target.md.

D7: Blizzard did the arithmetic in public

In 2020 Blizzard rebuilt the Ahn'Qiraj gate event for WoW Classic and explained why it was hard (Blizzard, Engineer's Workshop):

"In this group of 20, the server processes 380 packets (20 total players * 19 recipients = 380 packets)." … "1,500 players then 2,248,500 packets"

"What we faced is a polynomial problem, which means we can't solve it by throwing faster hardware at it because hardware's not exponentially better. Instead, we have to handcraft the optimization by deliberately choosing which data should be communicated to players and how often."

Check: 1,500 × 1,499 = 2,248,500. That is the same N(N − 1) fan-out from §3.

The lever is the latency budget

Each genre has a budget: how late the authoritative result can arrive before combat feels broken. Claypool & Claypool's measurements put it at about 100 ms for first-person shooters, 500 ms for third-person RPGs, and 1000 ms for omnipresent games (CACM 2006). Every MMO scaling trick spends that budget.

  • WoW batched on purpose for ten years. Blizzard's Celestalon, 2014: "Any action that one unit takes on another different unit used to be processed in batches every 400ms" (Blizzard forums). Players treated mutual Polymorphs and posthumous heals as quirks.
  • The global cooldown caps the action rate. Most abilities share a 1.5 s cooldown (0.75 s at the haste floor), so nobody acts more than about once a second.
  • No Lag compensation. A heal or a target-locked missile resolves against a unit ID on the server. Nothing aims at a position the shooter saw 80 ms ago, so there is no rewind buffer and no per-shot rewind cost.
  • Movement is sparse and event-driven. 2007 packet traces show WoW clients on TCP with inter-arrival peaks around 200 and 300 ms (Molnár & Szabó). Under the AQ load Blizzard went further: dropping facing updates and sending player movement "only whenever a player starts, stops, or uses keyboard movement". Blizzard has never published a movement rate in Hz.
  • EVE simulates at 1 Hz. "Each ballpark runs at a rate of one tick per second" (CCP Masterplan). When a node overloads, Time Dilation slows the game clock, down to 10% (CCP Veritas).
  • Split the crowd. WoW layers regions and shards zones (a WoW "shard" is a copy of one zone, not an Omega Shard); Wintergrasp queued at 120 per faction; Albion runs each zone on one thread and queues players proportionally per alliance.

They still break

The 2006 AQ gate opening put players in "a loop of logging in, disconnecting, and trying to get back online over a 12-hour period" (Blizzard). EVE's B-R5RB battle in 2014 ran at the 10% dilation floor for about 21 hours of real time to compute "just over 2 hours" of game time (CCP). Check: 21 h × 10% ≈ 2.1 h.

What a shooter can't borrow

Lever Why a bullet hell can't pull it
Low, event-driven movement rate Projectiles hit positions. Coarse remote motion means shots miss what the shooter saw.
400 ms server batching A dodge is decided in one or two Ticks. 400 ms is longer than a whole dodge.
Unit-ID targeting, no Lag compensation Aim is the skill. A hit has to be checked against where things were.
Time Dilation Twitch feel collapses at any dilation.
Culling distant characters You can't dodge bullets from enemies you can't see.
Layering, zone caps, queues This one transfers. Omega already caps per Instance.

So which levers can a bullet hell use? Only the ones from §3: shrink k (real AoI), send fewer bits per record, send less often, or split the Instance. To see how much room there is, we need to open up our own bytes.

5. Omega's wire format, bit by bit

Here is §3's formula with our real constants plugged in, and where every byte goes. Code references are to rust/protocol and rust/server. The full research, with line numbers, is omega-wire-format-and-cost.md; full layouts are in Appendix B.

Framing

Every packet is [u8 type][payload]. There is no length field, because ENet preserves datagram boundaries. Integers are little-endian. Bit fields are packed LSB-first, and any byte-sized write first pads the current partial byte, so headers stay byte-aligned and only the entity records form a true bitstream. Decoding is strict: underflow, a bad discriminant or trailing bytes is an error.

Positions, velocities and the cursor are trunc(v × 10) clamped to i16: 0.1-unit steps, truncated toward zero, the same rule the client uses so prediction matches. Angles are trunc(rad × 100).

Upstream: PlayerInput, 22 bytes, every Tick

Bytes Field Encoding
0 type = 2 u8
1 sequence u8, wraps at 256, echoed back for Reconciliation
2–3 input flags u16 bitfield, 9 of 16 bits used
4–5 aim angle i16, rad × 100
6–9 predicted position x, y 2 × i16, 0.1 u
10–13 predicted velocity x, y 2 × i16, 0.1 u/s
14–17 cursor x, y 2 × i16, 0.1 u (only read on the Tick an ability fires)
18–19 client render Tick u16, low 16 bits, input to Lag compensation
20–21 client RTT u16, ms

At 30 Hz that is 22 × 30 = 660 B/s of payload per player, constant even when the player is idle. On the wire each input datagram is 28 + 2 + 8 + 22 = 60 B, so 1.8 KB/s. The input isn't bit-packed. With 9-bit flags, a 10-bit angle, 15-bit coordinates and the cursor sent only when an ability fires, it would be about 13–14 B.

Downstream: the Snapshot

Original ASCII layout
Delta Snapshot header (16 B, byte-aligned)
┌──────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬───────┬────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ type │ server_tick  │ server_ms    │ flags │ baseline_tick  │ entity_count │
│ u8   │ u32          │ u32          │ u8    │ u32 (delta only)│ u16          │
└──────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴───────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘
then a bitstream of records, LSB-first, final byte zero-padded:

Moving player, position-only delta record = 49 bits
┌──────┬───────────┬──────┬──────────┬──────────┐
│ kind │ offset    │ mask │ qx       │ qy       │
│ 2 b  │ 10 b      │ 5 b  │ 16 b     │ 16 b     │
└──────┴───────────┴──────┴──────────┴──────────┘
  kind 0 = player (ids 1–999), 1 = projectile (15-bit offset),
  2 = monster, 3 = world effect (14-bit offsets)
F3 · original figure brief

[FIGURE F3 — new] Redraw the ASCII above as a proper bit-layout diagram: header bytes, then one record of each kind (player 49 b, projectile 54 b, monster 53 b), drawn to scale.

The typed id replaces an old u16 id + u8 type: a 2-bit kind plus an offset into that kind's id range. A player id costs 12 bits, a projectile 17, a monster 16. After the id comes a 5-bit change mask: POSITION, ANIMATION, FLAGS, REMOVED, FULL. The record carries only the fields the mask selects.

Record Player Projectile Monster
Baseline (full) 63 b 68 b 67 b
Delta, position only 49 b 54 b 53 b
Delta, FULL (entity new to this client) 68 b 73 b 72 b
Delta, REMOVED 17 b 22 b 21 b

So a moving entity costs 6–7 bytes per Tick, and the 32-bit absolute position is 60–65% of it.

What "delta" means here. Every field is absolute: a full quantized position, a full flags word. A delta record only omits fields that haven't changed since the state the server last sent that client. There's no arithmetic or XOR delta. Every 100 Ticks (3.3 s) the client gets a Baseline, a full Snapshot on reliable ch1, and acknowledges it. Since the correctness fixes, dependent delta Snapshots wait for the exact Baseline acknowledgement before they reference it (§6).

AoI and the byte budget

  • AoI: an entity enters a client's set at 1,000 units and leaves at 1,100 (hysteresis). A client's own entity is never culled.
  • Priority: importance (player 10, projectile 8, monster 4) plus Ticks since last sent, minus a distance penalty, plus a change bonus. Admission is greedy in priority order.
  • Budget: at most 1,200 B per delta Snapshot. Since the fixes this counts the header, rounding and pinned removal records, so the whole unreliable payload stays under 1,200 B.

Here is the punchline of this section. The Arena is 2,000 × 2,000 units. An AoI disc of radius 1,000 covers up to π × 1000² / 2000² = 78.5% of it from the centre. In a measured 50-bot run a bot saw on average 21.4 players and 35.7 projectiles, about 42% of everything in the Instance. In this Arena our AoI is a modest cull, not interest management. In §3's terms, k is still a fixed fraction of N, so we are on the N² branch.

Where the bytes go

The breakdown below comes from a local 50-bot run in which a scratch tally classified every received packet and every record with the real encoder.

[AUTHOR] Evidence caveat. This tally ran locally on commit 62fbfc3, before the correctness fixes, with the default (not Strategy) bot behaviour. The fixes changed no layout, so the bit costs stand. The fixes do add correctness traffic (exact-ACK waiting, recovery), so the shares are indicative. Fixed-build byte shares: [MEASURE].

Item, per bot per second B/s Share of downstream
Delta Snapshots (avg 384 B, max 1,057 B) 11,410 83.4%
· projectile records 7,466 54.5%
· player records 3,399 24.8%
· 16 B headers 475 3.5%
Baselines 142 1.0%
ActionConfirm (16 B per Tick, owner only) 475 3.5%
Game events (132 per second) 1,627 11.9%
· PROJECTILE_FIRED, 12 B, every shot in the Instance 1,125 8.2%
Total downstream application payload 13,687 100%
F4 · original figure brief

[FIGURE F4 — new] Stacked bar of the table above.

Within the Snapshots alone, projectiles are about 65% of the bytes and players 30%. Check the average Snapshot: 16 B header + (16.7 player records × 54.7 b + 37.1 projectile records × 54.2 b + 0.27 monster records × 53 b) / 8 ≈ 16 + 367 = 383 B, against 384.1 B measured.

Three things stand out:

  1. Projectiles are re-sent every Tick, even though their flight is deterministic. A projectile moves 400 u/s, 13.3 u per Tick, so every visible projectile costs a 54-bit position on every Tick: 202.5 B/s per visible projectile, per viewer. Its origin, direction and fire Tick are already in the PROJECTILE_FIRED Game event. So we pay twice: once for the reliable event, then per Tick for its whole life (1.4–2.0 s nominal range, about 0.9 s on average once hits and walls cut it short). This is the biggest waste in the protocol, and it's a design choice, not a bug.
  2. Game events go to every peer. They aren't AoI-filtered or budgeted. Every client pays for every shot fired anywhere in the Instance. That is an O(N) per-recipient term however small the AoI gets.
  3. About 1 KB/s per player is fixed before any other entity is drawn: header, ActionConfirm, the player's own record and a 1 Hz metrics packet.

On the wire, ENet and IP add about 74 B per Tick per peer downstream (one datagram: 28 B IP/UDP, 4 B ENet header, 8 B per unreliable command, 6 B per reliable event), about +16% on top of the payload. A 12-byte reliable PROJECTILE_FIRED carries a 6-byte command header and costs the client an 8-byte ACK going back.

D8: the cost model

Fitting per-entity coefficients to that run gives, per recipient, downstream payload:

R(N) ≈ 1.3 KB/s  +  0.42·(N−1)·157  +  0.42·N·1.7·209  +  30·N     [B/s]
     ≈ 1.3 KB/s  +  ~245 B/s · N
E(N) = N · R(N)   → quadratic total egress

The 0.42 is the visible fraction, 157 B/s is a visible player, 1.7 is projectile-seconds per player, 209 B/s is a visible projectile, and 30 B/s is the broadcast-event cost each player adds for every recipient. [D] The Snapshot alone reaches the 1,200 B budget when (1200 − 16) / ((0.42 × 157 + 0.42 × 1.7 × 209) / 30) ≈ 165 players. Past that the scheduler starts deferring records, and broadcast Game events keep growing without bound: about 15 KB/s per recipient at 500 players and 30 KB/s at 1000.

[AUTHOR] The model is fitted at N = 50 with default bots and extrapolated. Nothing in the fit was measured above 50. Keep the word "model".

6. How we load-tested it

A load test is only as honest as its generator and its pass gates. Ours found bugs before it found a ceiling, and several of the bugs were in the test itself.

Setup

  • Two Hetzner CAX11 hosts in the same Falkenstein zone, one for the game and one for the bots. Pinned release ARM builds. Unsigned dev-mode tickets, no API, no persistence, UDP restricted to the bot host.
  • The bots are real clients. omega-load-test links the same protocol and sim_core crates as the game, so every bot encodes real input and runs real prediction. It isn't a packet replayer.
  • Workloads: idle (connect only), movement, combat (always shooting), clustered (everyone converges on the origin) and Strategy, the gameplay-like one: target selection, orbiting at range, intercept aim with error, projectile dodging, sprint, dash and Class abilities.
  • Each cell: 30 Hz input, 100 ms join stagger, 60 s of warmup, then a 300-second measured window. One observation per cell, no repeats.
  • Pass gates: 30 Ticks per second held; every bot's input at ≥ 29.7 Hz both as offered and as seen on the wire; population held; delivery, decode and UDP error counters clean; received AoI correct. A requested population is not an achieved load.

Collection was compact: per-second host counters, exact window counters, a 1/64 UDP fingerprint sample for delivery estimates, no payloads. A compact bundle was 1.12 MiB against 110.5 MiB for full capture, 99% smaller.

Round 1: the first bugs

Before and during the first campaign (14 October 2026), the harness exposed:

  • The UDP adapter ignored ENet's requested socket buffers. The effective receive limit was the 212,992 B. After the fix, 524,288 B.
  • A cache/Baseline mismatch let omitted entities re-enter with partial records.
  • New entities couldn't recover if their first unreliable FULL record was lost.
  • Host maintenance silently restarted captures and invalidated the first Strategy 100 run.

Round 2: is it the server, or the bots?

The first Strategy 150 cell failed, and the failure said nothing about the server: the bot host sat at 97.8% of one core and offered about 18 inputs per second instead of 30. A profile found the Strategy bot's target search doing too much work. Searching the smaller visible-entity map restored every bot to 29.993–30.000 Hz offered, at 78.3% CPU, with the same choices.

Then we reproduced a 200-player ramp with more instrumentation. All 172,927 game-host receive-buffer errors matched the game socket's own drop counter: these were socket queue drops, not interface or checksum errors. Gaps between socket reads grew from about 26 ms to a maximum of 443 ms. Bytes of reliable retries grew from 132,337 to 13,688,810 across equal 9-second windows, about 100×. Raising the receive buffer to 4 MiB effective let all 200 players join, then collapsed with 159,266 drops. A bigger queue absorbs a burst. It doesn't add throughput.

Round 3: the correctness campaign

The author's rule for this article was that no result could rest on a build with known bugs. So we fixed them and reran. The fixes (merged in PR #44):

  1. Delta size accounting. The 1,200 B budget counted record bits only, so a full delta could reach 1,216 B plus pinned removals. The budget now counts the encoded packet.
  2. Exact Baseline ACK gating. Deltas referenced the last Baseline sent, not the last one acknowledged. Dependent deltas now wait for the exact ACK.
  3. Cross-channel retirement. An old ch0 delta could recreate an entity after a newer ch1 Baseline had removed it.
  4. Baseline decoder cap. Baselines now respect the decoder's entity-count limit.
  5. Recovery AoI filtering. Full-state recovery now uses AoI selection.
  6. Received-AoI measurement (ours). The bot checked a Snapshot's entity positions against the observer's position from a different moment. It now uses the observer position in the same Snapshot. Part of an earlier "AoI failure" was our checker.
  7. Tick-rate estimation (ours). See the sidebar.

The campaign took 23 attempts, 20 launched workloads, and produced 10 clean cells out of the 12 planned. That's a 43.5% attempt yield. Our own assessment calls it a campaign-management failure: too much effort went into repeated harness and storage failures without an early stopping budget.

Sidebar: a number that lied. [AUTHOR: keep or cut] An early report said the server ran at 32.9 Hz. It runs a fixed 30 Hz accumulator. The bot's estimator divided the Tick span (which included the spawn phase) by the fixed run length: 30 × 131.6 s / 120 s = 32.9. After the fix it pairs each Snapshot Tick span with its server-clock span. On the clean Strategy 150 cell it reports 29.99998120034632 Hz, and so fails the unchanged >= 30 criterion because of the 1 ms clock resolution, while the Tick log shows exactly 9,000 Ticks in 300 s. We kept both numbers and didn't round the failure into a pass. The 32.9 Hz report itself comes from a historical run whose raw data hasn't been retrieved yet (historical reports); the arithmetic is reproduced from code.

7. Results

Two builds produced results, and they don't mix:

  • Original build (game b1266c1, 14 Oct 2026): the first ladder and the five overload ramps, 512 KiB effective socket buffers.
  • Fixed build (game SHA-256 de92e120…, 22–24 Oct 2026): the clean correctness campaign, 4 MiB effective game socket buffers.

The fixed build that was load-tested is the campaign's binary. The fixes extracted to master were validated locally but not load-tested again.

The clean cells, fixed build

Each row is one 300-second observation after warmup. All held 30.0 Ticks per second and passed every campaign gate. (Accepted results audit.)

Workload 50 players, Tick-work p99 100 players 150 players
Idle — 8.02 ms not clean
Movement 5.56 ms 9.54 ms 13.61 ms
Combat 6.74 ms 14.61 ms —
Clustered 7.19 ms — —
Strategy 6.88 ms 14.15 ms 26.25 ms

Strategy 150, the headline pass. All 150 players stayed authenticated for 300 seconds after warmup. 9,000 Ticks, 30.0 Hz. Tick-work p99 26.25 ms of the 33.33 ms budget, maximum 58.0 ms, ten Ticks over budget. Every peer passed offered and wire cadence (29.81–29.99 Hz on the wire), delivery and received-AoI gates. Received AoI was checked over 203,603,817 matched positions, with zero violations. Correctness and UDP error counters were zero on both hosts.

It is one cell under its recorded conditions, not a capacity certificate. Those players weren't all fighting: the living population ranged from 102 to 143, and the median monster count was zero.

[D] The p99 grows faster than N, sometimes. Strategy p99 roughly doubled from 50 to 100 players (× 2.06) and grew × 1.86 from 100 to 150, for 1.5× the players. Fitting p99 ∝ N^a to each step gives a ≈ 1.04, then a ≈ 1.53. Movement gives a ≈ 0.78, then 0.88. These are single observations of a tail percentile, not a cost curve. Treat the exponents as a hint, not a measurement.

The original ladder and the N² in our bytes

The original build's ladder: Movement passed 50/100/150. Combat passed 50/100; Combat 150 failed (a ~99% CPU episode for about 11 seconds, then 135 bots disconnected). Clustered passed 50 and failed at 75 with kernel UDP errors. Strategy passed 50/100; 125 and 150 failed offered-load validation (the generator problem above), so they say nothing about the server.

Original Strategy 100: 30.000 Ticks per second, 29.981 Hz exact wire input, Tick-work p99 15.96 ms, game CPU mean 39.7% of one core, outbound 3,670,419.81 IP bytes/s.

D9, the N² in our bytes [D]. Outbound IP bytes per authenticated player-second, original build:

Strategy Outbound IP B/s Per player-second
50 1,093,347.36 21,866.95
100 3,670,419.81 36,704.20

Doubling N grew per-player bytes × 1.68 and total egress × 3.36. Pure k = N − 1 would give ×2 and ×4. Fixed per-player costs (input confirms, headers, the player's own record) are the likely reason it's less [D, not isolated].

[AUTHOR] Both rows are original-build. That build's byte counts include recovery traffic and the 16 B budget overshoot fixed later. Matched fixed-build outbound bytes per player-second: [MEASURE]. Don't use the fixed-build "39.66 KB/s" or "31.94 KiB/s" legacy figures here; they sum both directions over a different denominator.

D10, model against measurement [D]. The §5 model predicts about 26 KB/s of payload per client at N = 100. With ~16% wire overhead that is about 30.2 KB/s, against 36.7 KB/s measured: the measurement is about 22% higher. Plausible reasons, none isolated: the model was fitted to default bots, not Strategy bots (which dodge, sprint and use abilities); the original build sent extra FULL recovery records; outbound IP bytes include reliable retries and Baselines. The order of magnitude holds. The gap is unexplained.

Overload

The original-build ramps from §0, with the first second in which the game host recorded receive-buffer errors:

Requested Population at first game-host receive errors Game CPU then Ramp peak
200 131–139 56.8% 191
250 157–164 69.0% 185
500 156–162 76.2% 176
750 132–140 58.1% 180
999 150–157 64.1% 190

CPU is a one-second average, so a shorter stall or burst can overflow a queue while that second's average is below 100%. The first game CPU interval at ≥ 95% came later, at 176–191 players.

The fixed build's single Strategy 200 attempt reached all 200 players, then lost population to about 80 and aborted 28.7 seconds before measurement. It recorded 135,913 game-host and 299 bot-host receive-buffer errors. Because the bot host was losing packets too, the attempt cannot isolate a server ceiling. A follow-up to make the bot host's overload measurement trustworthy failed its own local test and stopped before any remote run (Strategy overload follow-up).

The strangest result: the fixed build's Idle 150 cell, where bots only connect and send input, did not pass. Every bot offered input at the right rate, but 113 of 150 peers fell below the 29.7 Hz gate on the wire, on both captures, while Strategy 150 passed. The cause is unknown. An attempt to instrument it failed its local overhead gate (+5.55% against ≤ 2%) and stopped (Idle150 follow-up).

D11: against the Valorant yardstick [D, inference]

D1 rescaled Valorant to about 128 players per core at 30 Hz. Original Strategy 100 ran 100 × 30 = 3,000 player-Ticks per second at 39.7% of a core: a naive 7,560 player-Ticks per core-second. Fixed Strategy 150 ran 4,500 player-Ticks per second on one serial loop. Both are the same order as Valorant's 3,840, from a 2D sim with no animation and no 3D traces. This comparison is loose: Valorant's figure is a provisioning target across a whole host, ours is one process's average or one thread's wall clock.

D12: transfer and money

At the original Strategy 100 rate, continuous use would move 3,670,419.81 × 86,400 × 30 = 9.51 TB per 30 days (decimal), or 115.75 TB per 365 days. That's arithmetic on a same-zone, old-build observation, not an invoice. Fixed-build external transfer, the monthly and yearly cost, and any 1000-CCU forecast: [MEASURE].

What we didn't get

The agreed matrix also had delay, jitter and loss profiles, Snapshot-rate and AoI-radius comparisons (Snapshot 15 Hz, AoI 600) and genuinely external clients. We have one native Combat 100 control and one 25 ms delay observation. The rest is [MEASURE], deferred to Stage 4.

8. Which wall did we hit? [PENDING]

[PENDING headline] Draft framing from the outline: "the same wall, with a twist: the receive path fails before the CPU does." Alternatives: "here is how far a 2D top-down game can push it", or "we found the wall, then found our test was part of it". Decide after reading §7.

What the data supports today:

  • On the original build, failure began in the receive path. Socket queue drops started at 131–164 players while process CPU averaged 57–76% of a core. Near-core CPU, lost players and join timeouts followed.
  • The diagnosis matched the drops to the game socket and saw read gaps and reliable retries grow during the failure: amplification after overflow. It did not prove what started it.
  • A larger buffer delayed the overflow without sustaining 200. Absorbing a burst isn't adding throughput.
  • On the fixed build, with 4 MiB buffers, 150 passed cleanly with p99 at 79% of the Tick budget.
  • The fixed build's limit is unknown. Its one overload attempt couldn't be measured.

Ranked hypotheses, none proven:

  1. The serial loop runs out of time. One thread services ENet, runs the Tick, encodes and flushes. While it is busy encoding, nobody reads the socket, so a burst of inbound datagrams has to fit in the kernel queue. Strategy 150's p99 at 26 ms leaves a 7 ms margin.
  2. Bursts between socket reads overflow the queue. Input from N clients arrives at 30 × N datagrams per second, plus ACKs for every reliable event (and reliable events grow with N).
  3. Reliable retries amplify the backlog. Once drops start, retransmits add load. The 100× growth in retry bytes fits this. Whether retries cause or follow overload isn't established.
  4. Our generator contributes. It did at Strategy 150 originally, and at Strategy 200 the bot host dropped packets too.

One coincidence worth noting, not claiming: the §5 model puts the 1,200 B Snapshot budget at about 165 players, inside the 131–164 receive-error onset. No causal link has been shown, the model is an extrapolation, and receive-side drops are about inbound traffic, not Snapshot size.

What 1000 would take

Mapped back to the levers in §2–§4:

  1. Make AoI shrink k. A 1,000-unit AoI in a 2,000-unit Arena shows ~42% of the Instance. Rust's k is 1–2% of N. Either the map grows with N or the radius shrinks.
  2. Stop re-sending deterministic projectiles. Send the fire event and the removal; let the client fly the bullet. That is about 54% of downstream at 50 bots.
  3. AoI-filter Game events. They're the only term that grows without bound after Snapshots cap.
  4. Get the Tick off one core. Encode each entity once per Tick and copy bits per recipient; serialise per recipient in parallel; or split the Instance (meshing, sharding).
  5. Read the socket off the Tick thread, so a long Tick doesn't leave the receive queue unattended.

None of these is implemented. Each one changes the game or the server, and each would need its own measurement.

9. Conclusion

The player cap isn't folklore. It's a fixed CPU budget per Tick set against work that grows as N · k, with k ≈ N − 1 whenever everyone can see everyone. Bit-packing and deltas buy constant factors. AoI changes the exponent, if the map lets it. Tab-target games escape by changing the game so the server can be late. Rust escapes by keeping k tiny, then hits a CPU wall at a few hundred. Battlefield keeps everyone relevant on purpose and pays in tick rate.

On a $7.59 box, our first build's join ramps broke near 190, right where the industry stops. Fixing our bugs, including the ones in our own test, got a clean 150. Past that the ceiling is unknown [PENDING: headline], and the honest version of this article says so.

The most transferable lesson might be the boring one. Before you trust a capacity number, prove that the generator offered the load, that the wire carried it, and that your checker measured what it claims. Ours didn't, at first.
